topics.title: TRANSACTIONS, CONCURRENCY AND RECOVERY
topics.description: Learn how database systems maintain correctness and reliability when multiple operations execute concurrently or when failures occur. This topic covers transactions, ACID properties, schedules, serializability, concurrency anomalies, locks, two-phase locking, deadlocks, timestamps, optimistic concurrency, recovery techniques, logging, checkpoints, undo, redo, and crash recovery.

sections.title: What Is a Database Transaction?
sections.content:
A transaction is a logical unit of database work consisting of one or more operations that should be treated as a single unit from the perspective of correctness.

For example, transferring money between two bank accounts requires at least two changes:

```text
Account A -> Deduct ₹1000
Account B -> Add ₹1000
```

Both operations belong to the same transaction. If the debit succeeds but the credit fails, the transaction should not leave the database in a state where the money has disappeared.

Transactions provide a foundation for maintaining database consistency while applications perform complex operations.

sections.title: Transaction Operations
sections.content:
A transaction can contain several types of database operations, including reads and writes.

Conceptually:

```text
BEGIN TRANSACTION
    READ account A
    WRITE account A
    READ account B
    WRITE account B
COMMIT
```

The transaction normally ends with either `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`.

`COMMIT` makes the transaction's changes permanent according to the database's durability guarantees. `ROLLBACK` cancels the transaction's changes according to the database's transaction semantics.

sections.title: Transaction States
sections.content:
A transaction can move through several states during its lifecycle.

Common states include:

```text
Active
  |
  v
Partially Committed
  |
  v
Committed
```

If an error occurs, the transaction may move toward an aborted state:

```text
Active
  |
  v
Failed
  |
  v
Aborted
```

A committed transaction has successfully completed. An aborted transaction has had its effects rolled back or otherwise resolved according to the recovery process.

sections.title: ACID Properties
sections.content:
The reliability of transactions is commonly described using the ACID properties.

```text
Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
```

Atomicity means the transaction is treated as an all-or-nothing unit.

Consistency means a successfully completed transaction preserves the database's defined integrity rules.

Isolation controls how concurrent transactions interact with each other.

Durability means committed changes are intended to survive failures according to the database system's durability guarantees.

sections.title: Atomicity
sections.content:
Atomicity means that the operations belonging to a transaction are treated as one logical unit.

Consider a bank transfer:

```text
Debit A
Credit B
```

If the credit operation fails, atomicity requires the system to prevent the transaction from leaving only the debit behind.

The database can use mechanisms such as transaction logs and recovery processing to undo incomplete changes after failures.

sections.title: Consistency
sections.content:
Consistency means that a transaction should move the database from one valid state to another valid state according to the database's constraints and application rules.

For example, if an account balance cannot be negative according to a business constraint, a successful transaction should not violate that rule.

Consistency depends on both database-enforced constraints and application-level business rules. The DBMS can enforce structural constraints such as primary keys and foreign keys, while application logic may be responsible for additional business rules.

sections.title: Isolation
sections.content:
Isolation determines how the operations of concurrently executing transactions are exposed to one another.

Without appropriate isolation, one transaction could observe intermediate or conflicting changes made by another transaction.

For example, if one transaction is updating an account balance while another transaction reads that balance, the database must follow a defined isolation policy.

Isolation does not necessarily mean that transactions execute one after another. Database systems use concurrency-control mechanisms to allow parallel execution while preserving required correctness properties.

sections.title: Durability
sections.content:
Durability means that once a transaction is committed, its effects should survive an appropriate system failure according to the database's guarantees.

Databases commonly use persistent storage and transaction logging to support durability.

A simplified flow is:

```text
Transaction
    |
    v
Commit
    |
    v
Durable Log / Storage
    |
    v
Recovery After Failure
```

Durability is closely related to recovery mechanisms, write-ahead logging, checkpoints, replication, and storage reliability.

sections.title: Schedules
sections.content:
A schedule describes the order in which operations from one or more transactions are executed.

Suppose transaction T1 performs `read(A)` and `write(A)`, while T2 performs `read(B)` and `write(B)`. A schedule specifies how these operations are interleaved.

A serial schedule executes transactions one after another:

```text
T1 -> T1 -> T1 -> T2 -> T2 -> T2
```

A concurrent schedule interleaves operations:

```text
T1 -> T2 -> T1 -> T2 -> T1 -> T2
```

Concurrency improves resource utilization, but the interleaving must be controlled so that correctness is preserved.

sections.title: Serial Schedule
sections.content:
A serial schedule executes one transaction completely before starting another.

For example:

```text
T1:
READ(A)
WRITE(A)
COMMIT

T2:
READ(B)
WRITE(B)
COMMIT
```

Serial execution is straightforward to reason about because transactions do not interfere with one another.

However, forcing every transaction to execute serially can reduce concurrency and database throughput. Concurrency-control techniques aim to provide the benefits of parallel execution while preserving appropriate correctness properties.

sections.title: Concurrent Schedule
sections.content:
A concurrent schedule interleaves operations from multiple transactions.

For example:

```text
T1: READ(A)
T2: READ(B)
T1: WRITE(A)
T2: WRITE(B)
T1: COMMIT
T2: COMMIT
```

Concurrent execution allows database resources such as CPU, memory, storage, and network connections to be used more efficiently.

The challenge is that operations from different transactions may access the same data. Without concurrency control, this can lead to incorrect results.

sections.title: Serializability
sections.content:
Serializability is a correctness criterion for concurrent schedules. A concurrent schedule is serializable if its effect is equivalent to some valid serial execution of the same transactions.

The idea is:

```text
Concurrent Schedule
        |
        v
Equivalent Result
        |
        v
Some Serial Schedule
```

Serializability allows databases to execute transactions concurrently while preserving the logical behavior of a serial execution.

Conflict serializability is one of the most commonly studied forms.

sections.title: Conflict Serializability
sections.content:
A schedule is conflict-serializable when it can be transformed into a serial schedule by swapping non-conflicting operations without changing the result.

Two operations conflict when:

- They belong to different transactions.
- They access the same data item.
- At least one operation is a write.

Examples of conflicts include:

```text
READ(A)  vs WRITE(A)
WRITE(A) vs READ(A)
WRITE(A) vs WRITE(A)
```

Two reads of the same item do not conflict because neither modifies the data.

sections.title: Precedence Graph
sections.content:
A precedence graph can be used to test conflict serializability.

Each transaction is represented as a node. If an operation from T1 conflicts with a later operation from T2 on the same data item, an edge is added from T1 to T2.

```text
T1 ----> T2
```

If the resulting graph contains a cycle, the schedule is not conflict-serializable.

If the graph is acyclic, a topological ordering of the transactions can provide an equivalent serial order.

sections.title: Recoverable Schedules
sections.content:
A schedule is recoverable when a transaction does not commit before another transaction whose changes it has read has committed.

For example, if T2 reads data written by T1, T2 should not commit before T1 commits.

```text
T1: WRITE(A)
T2: READ(A)
T1: COMMIT
T2: COMMIT
```

This ordering avoids committing a transaction based on data produced by a transaction that might later abort.

sections.title: Cascading Rollback
sections.content:
A cascading rollback can occur when one transaction reads data written by another transaction that later aborts.

For example:

```text
T1: WRITE(A)
T2: READ(A)
T1: ROLLBACK
```

Because T2 used data produced by T1, T2 may also need to be rolled back.

Cascading rollbacks can propagate through multiple transactions. Database systems can use stricter schedules, locking, or isolation mechanisms to avoid reading uncommitted data.

sections.title: Concurrency Problems
sections.content:
Concurrent transactions can produce several well-known anomalies when insufficient isolation is provided.

Important problems include:

- Lost update.
- Dirty read.
- Non-repeatable read.
- Phantom read.
- Incorrect summary or inconsistent analysis.

The exact anomalies permitted depend on the database system and transaction isolation level.

Understanding these problems is essential because application bugs caused by concurrency can be difficult to reproduce and may only appear under production load.

sections.title: Lost Update
sections.content:
A lost update occurs when two transactions read the same value and then update it based on their separate copies, causing one update to overwrite the other.

For example:

```text
Initial balance = 100

T1 reads 100
T2 reads 100
T1 writes 150
T2 writes 120

Final value = 120
```

The effect of T1's update has been lost.

Locking, optimistic version checks, appropriate isolation, or atomic database operations can be used to prevent this problem.

sections.title: Dirty Read
sections.content:
A dirty read occurs when one transaction reads data written by another transaction before that transaction has committed.

Example:

```text
T1: WRITE(A = 500)
T2: READ(A = 500)
T1: ROLLBACK
```

T2 read a value that was never committed.

Isolation levels such as Read Committed prevent dirty reads in systems that implement the standard semantics for that isolation level.

sections.title: Non-Repeatable Read
sections.content:
A non-repeatable read occurs when a transaction reads the same row more than once and receives different committed values because another transaction modified and committed the row between the reads.

```text
T1: READ(A = 100)
T2: UPDATE(A = 150)
T2: COMMIT
T1: READ(A = 150)
```

The same transaction observed different values for the same row.

Higher isolation levels can provide stronger guarantees against this behavior.

sections.title: Phantom Read
sections.content:
A phantom read occurs when a transaction executes the same range-based query twice and finds a different set of rows because another transaction inserted, deleted, or otherwise changed rows matching the query condition.

For example:

```text
T1: SELECT orders WHERE amount > 1000
T2: INSERT order with amount = 1500
T2: COMMIT
T1: SELECT orders WHERE amount > 1000
```

The second query may return an additional row.

Preventing phantoms can require stronger isolation or database-specific locking mechanisms.

sections.title: Transaction Isolation Levels
sections.content:
Common SQL isolation levels are:

```text
Read Uncommitted
Read Committed
Repeatable Read
Serializable
```

They provide different trade-offs between concurrency and consistency.

A simplified view is:

```text
Stronger isolation
        ^
        |
   Serializable
   Repeatable Read
   Read Committed
   Read Uncommitted
        |
        v
Higher potential concurrency
```

The exact behavior of each level can differ between database engines, especially because some systems use locking while others use multi-version concurrency control.

sections.title: Read Uncommitted
sections.content:
Read Uncommitted provides the weakest commonly defined isolation level. A transaction may be allowed to read data that another transaction has not yet committed.

This can allow dirty reads and other concurrency anomalies.

It can provide high concurrency, but the application must tolerate weaker consistency.

The actual behavior depends on the database implementation, and some database engines may not expose exactly the same behavior even when they use the same isolation-level terminology.

sections.title: Read Committed
sections.content:
Read Committed ensures that a transaction does not read uncommitted changes from other transactions under the standard semantics.

It prevents dirty reads, but repeated reads can still observe different committed values if another transaction modifies the row between reads.

```text
T1: READ(A = 100)
T2: UPDATE(A = 200)
T2: COMMIT
T1: READ(A = 200)
```

Read Committed is widely used because it provides stronger consistency than Read Uncommitted while allowing substantial concurrency.

sections.title: Repeatable Read
sections.content:
Repeatable Read provides stronger guarantees for repeated reads of the same data than Read Committed.

The precise behavior regarding phantom rows varies between database implementations and concurrency-control mechanisms.

Some systems use multi-version concurrency control, while others may use different combinations of locks and snapshots.

When selecting an isolation level, developers should understand the guarantees of their specific database system rather than relying only on the isolation-level name.

sections.title: Serializable Isolation
sections.content:
Serializable is the strongest standard SQL isolation level. Its goal is to provide behavior equivalent to some serial execution of concurrent transactions.

This can prevent a broad range of concurrency anomalies, but stronger isolation may reduce concurrency or increase contention depending on the implementation.

A system can achieve serializable behavior through different techniques, including locking or serialization mechanisms based on versioned data.

Serializable isolation is useful when correctness requirements demand strong guarantees, but it should be evaluated against workload and performance requirements.

sections.title: Locks
sections.content:
Locks are a concurrency-control mechanism used to coordinate access to database resources.

Two common lock modes are:

```text
Shared Lock   -> Used for reading
Exclusive Lock -> Used for writing
```

Multiple transactions may be able to hold compatible shared locks simultaneously, while an exclusive lock generally prevents conflicting access.

Lock behavior varies by database engine, but the core idea is to prevent incompatible operations from occurring at the same time.

sections.title: Shared and Exclusive Locks
sections.content:
A shared lock is commonly associated with reading, while an exclusive lock is associated with modifying data.

Conceptually:

```text
Shared + Shared       -> Often compatible
Shared + Exclusive    -> Conflict
Exclusive + Exclusive -> Conflict
```

The exact compatibility matrix depends on the database system and lock type.

Understanding shared and exclusive locks helps explain how databases prevent conflicting operations from corrupting or incorrectly updating shared data.

sections.title: Two-Phase Locking
sections.content:
Two-Phase Locking, or 2PL, is a concurrency-control protocol with two phases.

```text
Growing Phase
-> Acquire locks
-> Do not release locks

Shrinking Phase
-> Release locks
-> Do not acquire new locks
```

The protocol helps guarantee conflict serializability under its standard assumptions.

A stricter variant, Strict Two-Phase Locking, holds write locks until the transaction commits or aborts. This can simplify recovery and prevent certain cascading effects.

sections.title: Deadlocks
sections.content:
A deadlock occurs when transactions wait for each other indefinitely.

For example:

```text
T1 holds Lock(A)
T2 holds Lock(B)

T1 waits for B
T2 waits for A
```

Neither transaction can proceed because each is waiting for the other.

Database systems can handle deadlocks using detection and rollback, prevention strategies, timeouts, or other engine-specific techniques.

sections.title: Deadlock Detection
sections.content:
Deadlocks can be represented using a wait-for graph.

Each transaction is represented by a node. An edge from T1 to T2 means T1 is waiting for a resource held by T2.

```text
T1 ----> T2
 ^        |
 |        v
 +--------+
```

A cycle in the wait-for graph indicates a deadlock.

A database can resolve the deadlock by selecting one transaction as a victim, rolling it back, and allowing the remaining transaction to continue.

sections.title: Deadlock Prevention
sections.content:
Deadlock prevention attempts to ensure that circular waiting cannot occur.

Common strategies include:

- Acquiring locks in a consistent global order.
- Using transaction priorities.
- Aborting transactions that violate a waiting rule.
- Using timeouts.

A simple application-level technique is to access shared resources in a consistent order. For example, if transactions must update two accounts, always acquire the lower account ID before the higher account ID.

This does not replace database-level concurrency control, but consistent ordering can reduce deadlock risk.

sections.title: Timestamp Ordering
sections.content:
Timestamp-ordering protocols assign transactions timestamps and use those timestamps to determine whether operations are allowed.

The basic idea is that transactions should behave consistently with their timestamp order.

For example:

```text
T1 timestamp = 10
T2 timestamp = 20
```

If an operation would violate the required ordering, the database may reject or roll back the transaction.

Timestamp-based concurrency control provides an alternative to lock-based protocols.

sections.title: Optimistic Concurrency Control
sections.content:
Optimistic concurrency control assumes conflicts are relatively uncommon. Transactions execute without acquiring traditional locks for every operation and validate whether conflicts occurred before committing.

A simplified process is:

```text
Read / Execute
      |
      v
Validation
      |
   +--+--+
   |     |
Success  Conflict
   |     |
Commit  Abort/Retry
```

Optimistic locking with a version column is a common application-level example.

This approach can work well when contention is low, but frequent conflicts can lead to repeated retries.

sections.title: Multi-Version Concurrency Control
sections.content:
Multi-Version Concurrency Control, or MVCC, maintains multiple versions of data so that readers and writers can often proceed with less direct blocking.

Conceptually:

```text
Row A
 |
 +-- Version 1
 |
 +-- Version 2
 |
 +-- Version 3
```

A transaction can read the version appropriate for its visibility rules while another transaction creates a newer version.

MVCC is used by several modern database systems, although implementation details differ significantly between engines.

Understanding MVCC helps explain why some databases can support concurrent reads and writes without using traditional blocking behavior for every read.

sections.title: What Is Database Recovery?
sections.content:
Database recovery is the process of restoring the database to a correct state after failures.

Failures can include:

- Transaction failures.
- System crashes.
- Power failures.
- Storage failures.
- Software failures.
- Other infrastructure problems.

A recovery mechanism must determine which operations were successfully committed and which incomplete operations need to be undone or completed.

Transaction logs are central to many database recovery systems.

sections.title: Types of Database Failures
sections.content:
Database systems can experience different types of failures.

A transaction failure affects an individual transaction, such as a constraint violation or application error.

A system crash can interrupt multiple active transactions while database files remain available after restart.

A media or storage failure can damage or make persistent database data unavailable.

Different failures require different recovery strategies. Transaction rollback may be enough for a logical error, while storage failure may require backups and additional recovery infrastructure.

sections.title: Transaction Log
sections.content:
A transaction log records information about database changes so the DBMS can recover from failures.

A simplified log might contain:

```text
<T1 START>
<T1, A, old=100, new=150>
<T1 COMMIT>
```

The exact log format varies by database system.

During recovery, the DBMS can use log records to determine which changes need to be redone and which incomplete changes need to be undone.

sections.title: Write-Ahead Logging
sections.content:
Write-Ahead Logging, or WAL, is a recovery principle in which the relevant log information is written to durable storage before the corresponding data changes are considered durable.

Conceptually:

```text
Change Data
    |
    v
Write Log First
    |
    v
Persist Data
```

This allows the recovery process to reconstruct or undo changes after a crash.

Many modern database systems use some form of write-ahead logging, although implementation details differ.

sections.title: Undo and Redo
sections.content:
Recovery commonly involves two fundamental ideas: undo and redo.

Undo reverses changes from transactions that should not remain, such as transactions that failed before committing.

Redo reapplies changes from committed transactions whose data pages may not have been fully persisted before a crash.

```text
UNDO -> Remove effects that should not remain
REDO -> Reapply committed effects when needed
```

The exact recovery algorithm depends on the database system's logging and storage architecture.

sections.title: Checkpointing
sections.content:
A checkpoint records a recovery point that allows the database to reduce the amount of log information that must be processed after a crash.

Without checkpoints, recovery may need to examine a very large portion of the transaction log.

Conceptually:

```text
Log ---- Log ---- Log ---- CHECKPOINT ---- Log ---- Crash
                                      |
                                      v
                              Recovery starts
                              with checkpoint
```

Checkpoint mechanisms differ between database systems, but the general purpose is to make recovery more efficient.

sections.title: Crash Recovery
sections.content:
After a system crash, the database must determine which transactions were committed, which were incomplete, and which changes need to be restored.

A simplified recovery process can be represented as:

```text
Database Crash
      |
      v
Read Recovery Information
      |
      v
Identify Committed / Incomplete Transactions
      |
      +----> REDO committed changes when required
      |
      +----> UNDO incomplete changes when required
      |
      v
Database returns to a consistent state
```

Real database engines use sophisticated logging and recovery algorithms to perform this process efficiently.

sections.title: Recovery Using Backups
sections.content:
Transaction logs help with many logical and system failures, but serious storage failures may require restoring database backups.

A recovery strategy can involve:

```text
Full Backup
     |
     v
Incremental / Log Backups
     |
     v
Restore
     |
     v
Replay Required Changes
```

A production backup strategy should define how frequently backups are taken, how long they are retained, where they are stored, and how recovery is tested.

A backup that has never been tested through an actual restore process should not be assumed to provide reliable recovery.

sections.title: Point-in-Time Recovery
sections.content:
Point-in-time recovery allows a database to be restored to a specific time using a suitable base backup and transaction logs.

For example, if an accidental deletion occurred at 14:30, a recovery strategy may allow the database to be restored to a point immediately before the mistake.

```text
Backup
  |
  +--- Log --- Log --- Log --- Target Time
                              |
                              v
                       Restore Database
```

The exact capabilities and procedures depend on the database system and backup architecture.

sections.title: Transactions in Application Code
sections.content:
Application code should define transaction boundaries around meaningful business operations.

For example, an order-placement workflow may require several related operations:

```text
Begin Transaction
    Create Order
    Reserve Inventory
    Create Payment Record
Commit
```

If one operation fails, the application may need to roll back the complete transaction.

Transactions should not be made unnecessarily large because long transactions can hold locks or versions for extended periods and increase resource usage.

sections.title: Transaction Propagation
sections.content:
In application frameworks, multiple service methods may participate in the same database transaction. Transaction propagation determines how a method behaves when a transaction already exists.

Conceptually:

```text
Service A
  |
  +---- Transaction
          |
          +---- Service B
          |
          +---- Repository
```

Depending on the framework and configuration, a nested service call may join the existing transaction, create a separate transaction, or use another propagation behavior.

Understanding transaction boundaries is important in layered applications because an apparently small method call may participate in a larger business transaction.

sections.title: Idempotency and Transactions
sections.content:
Idempotency means that repeating an operation produces the same intended result rather than creating unintended duplicate effects.

This is particularly important when applications retry operations after timeouts or transient failures.

For example, blindly retrying a payment creation request could potentially create duplicate records if the first request actually committed but the response was lost.

Database transactions provide atomicity, but application-level idempotency often requires additional mechanisms such as unique business keys, idempotency tokens, or carefully designed state transitions.

sections.title: Common Transaction and Recovery Mistakes
sections.content:
Common mistakes include:

- Treating a multi-step business operation as several unrelated transactions.
- Keeping transactions open while performing slow external operations.
- Assuming all isolation levels behave identically across database systems.
- Ignoring deadlocks and retry requirements.
- Reading uncommitted data without understanding the consequences.
- Retrying non-idempotent operations blindly.
- Assuming a commit guarantees recovery from every type of storage failure.
- Taking backups without testing restoration.
- Ignoring transaction-log growth.
- Holding locks for longer than necessary.
- Using stronger isolation everywhere without considering contention and throughput.

sections.title: Choosing a Concurrency Strategy
sections.content:
Different workloads benefit from different concurrency-control approaches.

Use database locking when conflicting operations need strong coordination. Use optimistic concurrency when conflicts are relatively rare and retries are acceptable. MVCC can provide efficient concurrent reads and writes in systems designed around multiple data versions.

The decision should consider:

- Conflict frequency.
- Transaction duration.
- Read/write ratio.
- Consistency requirements.
- Database implementation.
- Expected workload.
- Acceptable retry rate.

There is no single concurrency strategy that is optimal for every application.

sections.title: Transactions, Concurrency and Recovery in Practice
sections.content:
A reliable database application combines transaction management, concurrency control, and recovery rather than treating them as isolated concepts.

For example, an order-processing system may use:

```text
Application Request
        |
        v
Transaction
        |
        +---- Read Inventory
        |
        +---- Update Inventory
        |
        +---- Create Order
        |
        +---- Record Payment State
        |
        v
Commit
        |
        v
Transaction Log
        |
        v
Recovery if Failure Occurs
```

Concurrency control ensures simultaneous orders do not incorrectly modify shared inventory. Transactions provide atomicity across related operations. Logging and recovery allow the database to recover correctly after failures.

sections.title: Why Transactions, Concurrency and Recovery Matter
sections.content:
Transactions, concurrency control, and recovery form the foundation of reliable database systems. Transactions define logical units of work, concurrency control coordinates simultaneous operations, and recovery protects the database when transactions or infrastructure fail.

The most important practical concepts are ACID properties, serializability, isolation levels, locking, deadlock handling, optimistic concurrency, MVCC, transaction logging, write-ahead logging, checkpoints, undo, redo, and backup-based recovery.

Understanding these concepts helps developers design applications that remain correct not only when everything works normally, but also when many users access the system simultaneously or failures occur during critical operations.

topics.shortDescription: Learn database transactions, ACID properties, schedules, serializability, isolation levels, locking, deadlocks, concurrency control, logging, checkpoints, undo, redo, and crash recovery.

modules.title: Storage, Indexing and Query Processing
modules.description: File organization, indexes, query execution, cost, optimization, and relational operation processing.

topics.title: STORAGE, INDEXING AND QUERY PROCESSING
topics.description: Learn how database systems store data on disk, organize records into pages and files, build indexes for faster access, and execute SQL queries efficiently. This topic covers storage hierarchy, pages, records, file organization, heap files, sorted files, primary and secondary indexes, dense and sparse indexes, B-trees, B+ trees, hash indexes, clustered indexes, composite indexes, query execution plans, relational operators, query optimization, cost estimation, and practical performance tuning.

sections.title: Why Storage and Query Processing Matter
sections.content:
A database does much more than store rows. It must decide where data is stored, how records are organized, how indexes locate records, and how SQL queries are converted into efficient execution plans.

Consider:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 101;
```

The database could scan every order, or it could use an index on `customer_id` to locate matching rows quickly.

Understanding storage and query processing explains why two logically equivalent SQL queries can have very different performance characteristics.

sections.title: Database Storage Hierarchy
sections.content:
Database systems operate across multiple levels of storage, each with different capacity, latency, and cost.

A simplified hierarchy is:

```text
CPU Registers
    ↓
CPU Cache
    ↓
RAM
    ↓
SSD / NVMe
    ↓
HDD
    ↓
Remote / Backup Storage
```

CPU memory is extremely fast but limited. Persistent storage is slower but can retain large amounts of data.

Database performance is heavily influenced by how often data must move between these layers. Reducing unnecessary disk or storage I/O is one of the most important goals of database optimization.

sections.title: Pages and Blocks
sections.content:
Databases usually transfer data between persistent storage and memory in fixed-size units commonly called pages or blocks.

Instead of reading one row at a time from storage, a DBMS generally loads a page containing multiple records into memory.

```text
Disk
+-------------------------+
| Page 1                  |
| Record | Record | ...   |
+-------------------------+
| Page 2                  |
| Record | Record | ...   |
+-------------------------+
```

Page size is database-engine dependent. The important concept is that storage access happens in blocks, so the number of pages that must be read can be more important than the number of individual rows.

sections.title: Records and Tuples
sections.content:
A table row is represented internally as a record or tuple. A record contains the values belonging to its columns.

For example:

```text
Customer
+----+----------+-------------------+
| ID | Name     | Email             |
+----+----------+-------------------+
| 1  | Amit     | amit@example.com  |
+----+----------+-------------------+
```

The physical representation of a record can contain additional metadata such as record identifiers, null information, transaction information, or pointers depending on the database engine.

The logical row exposed by SQL does not necessarily correspond directly to the exact physical bytes stored on disk.

sections.title: Pages, Records and Row Layout
sections.content:
A database page typically contains multiple records along with page-level metadata.

A simplified representation is:

```text
+----------------------------------+
| Page Header                      |
+----------------------------------+
| Record 1                         |
+----------------------------------+
| Record 2                         |
+----------------------------------+
| Record 3                         |
+----------------------------------+
| Free Space                      |
+----------------------------------+
```

The exact layout depends on the storage engine.

Variable-length columns, NULL values, alignment, record headers, and deleted records can all influence how much data fits into a page. This affects how many pages a query must read.

sections.title: Disk I/O and Database Performance
sections.content:
A query that requires many storage reads can be significantly slower than one that can obtain most of its data from memory or a small number of pages.

For example:

```text
Table scan
100,000 rows
    ↓
Many pages read

Index lookup
Search index
    ↓
Few index pages
    ↓
Required data pages
```

Modern SSDs are much faster than traditional disks, but storage access is still generally more expensive than accessing data already available in memory.

This is why database optimizers consider I/O and why indexes and buffer caches can have a major impact on performance.

sections.title: Buffer Pool and Database Cache
sections.content:
A DBMS usually maintains memory structures that cache frequently accessed database pages. In many systems this is called a buffer pool or buffer cache.

Conceptually:

```text
Storage
   ↓
Buffer Pool
   ↓
Query Execution
```

If a required page is already in memory, the database may avoid a storage read.

Frequently accessed indexes and table pages can therefore remain in memory and serve repeated queries quickly.

The exact caching architecture varies by database engine, but the general principle is the same: memory is used to reduce expensive persistent-storage access.

sections.title: Database File Organization
sections.content:
A table's records must be physically organized in one or more files or storage structures.

Common conceptual organizations include:

- Heap files.
- Sorted or sequential files.
- Hash-organized files.
- Clustered storage structures.

The choice affects insertion speed, range queries, point lookups, and the usefulness of indexes.

For example, an organization optimized for fast sequential access may not be ideal for frequent random lookups.

sections.title: Heap File Organization
sections.content:
In a heap file, records are not maintained in a particular ordering based on a search key.

A simplified representation is:

```text
Page 1: Record 7, Record 2, Record 10
Page 2: Record 4, Record 1, Record 8
Page 3: Record 5, Record 3, Record 9
```

Heap organization can make insertion relatively simple because a new record can be placed where free space is available.

However, searching for a specific value without an appropriate index may require scanning many pages.

sections.title: Sorted File Organization
sections.content:
In a sorted file organization, records are maintained according to a search key.

For example:

```text
Customer ID
101
105
110
115
120
```

Sorted storage can make sequential processing and range access efficient.

However, maintaining physical order during frequent inserts and deletes can be expensive. Database systems often use indexes and storage structures that provide ordered access without requiring the entire table to be physically reorganized after every modification.

sections.title: What Is an Index?
sections.content:
An index is an auxiliary data structure that helps a database locate rows without scanning the entire table.

For example:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id
ON orders(customer_id);
```

Without an index, the database may need to inspect many rows to find matching values.

With an appropriate index, the optimizer may navigate the index to identify relevant records and then fetch the required rows.

Indexes improve some reads but consume storage and add maintenance work to inserts, updates, and deletes.

sections.title: How an Index Works
sections.content:
An index stores search-related information separately from the full table data.

A simplified structure might look like:

```text
Index Key       Record Location
---------       ---------------
101             -> Row/Page A
105             -> Row/Page C
110             -> Row/Page B
```

The database searches the index instead of examining every table row.

The exact structure depends on the index type. B-tree and B+ tree structures are widely used for ordered access, while hash indexes can be useful for equality-based lookups in systems that support them.

sections.title: Index Lookup vs Full Table Scan
sections.content:
Suppose a table contains one million orders:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE order_id = 900001;
```

A full table scan may inspect a large number of pages.

An index on `order_id` may allow the database to navigate directly toward the matching record.

However, an index is not automatically faster. If a query returns a very large percentage of the table, scanning the table sequentially may be cheaper than performing many random lookups.

The optimizer decides based on statistics, estimated costs, available indexes, and the query structure.

sections.title: Primary and Secondary Indexes
sections.content:
An index associated with the table's primary ordering or primary key is often described as a primary index in database theory. A secondary index provides another access path based on a different search attribute.

For example:

```text
Primary key: order_id
Secondary index: customer_id
Secondary index: order_date
```

The terminology and physical implementation vary by database system, so theoretical terms should not be confused with vendor-specific index types.

A table can have multiple useful secondary indexes when queries frequently search by different columns.

sections.title: Dense and Sparse Indexes
sections.content:
A dense index contains an index entry for every relevant search-key value or record, depending on the design.

A sparse index contains fewer entries and relies on an underlying ordered organization to locate the required region.

Conceptually:

```text
Dense:
101 -> row
102 -> row
103 -> row
104 -> row

Sparse:
101 -> page
103 -> page
105 -> page
```

Dense indexes can provide direct lookup information but may consume more storage. Sparse indexes can be smaller but require additional searching within the underlying data structure.

Modern database indexes often use implementation-specific structures, so these concepts are especially useful for understanding database indexing theory.

sections.title: B-Tree Index
sections.content:
A B-tree is a balanced tree structure designed to support efficient searching, insertion, and deletion while keeping the tree height relatively small.

Conceptually:

```text
             [50]
            /    \
       [20,30]   [70,90]
```

Balanced tree structures reduce the number of levels that must be traversed to locate a key.

Database systems use B-tree family structures because they work well with persistent storage and support ordered operations such as equality searches, range searches, and sorting.

sections.title: B+ Tree Index
sections.content:
A B+ tree is a balanced tree structure commonly used in database indexing. Internal nodes guide searches, while leaf nodes contain the searchable entries and are typically linked for efficient ordered traversal.

Conceptually:

```text
             [50]
            /    \
       [10,20]   [60,80]
          |          |
       leaf -----> leaf
```

The linked leaf level is particularly useful for range queries.

For example:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE order_id BETWEEN 1000 AND 2000;
```

The database can locate the first matching key and then traverse subsequent leaf entries efficiently.

sections.title: Why B+ Trees Work Well for Databases
sections.content:
B+ trees have several properties that make them useful for database indexes.

They maintain balance, keep the height relatively small, support ordered traversal, and can store many keys per page.

A high branching factor means a large number of keys can be represented at each level:

```text
             Root
          /   |   |   \
       Node Node Node Node
       /|\   /|\   /|\
    Leaf Leaf Leaf Leaf
```

Because database pages can contain many index entries, the number of storage accesses needed to reach a leaf can remain relatively small even for large tables.

sections.title: Hash Indexes
sections.content:
A hash index uses a hash function to map search keys to buckets.

Conceptually:

```text
Hash(key)
    |
    v
Bucket
    |
    v
Matching records
```

Hash indexes are naturally suited to equality lookups such as:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE email = 'user@example.com';
```

They are generally not designed for ordered range traversal in the same way as B-tree family indexes.

Support and implementation details depend on the database engine.

sections.title: Clustered Index
sections.content:
A clustered index determines or strongly influences the physical organization of table data according to the database engine's storage model.

A simplified conceptual layout is:

```text
Index order
100
110
120
130

Data pages follow a related order
```

Clustered organization can make range queries efficient because related records may be stored close together.

A critical point is that the exact meaning of a clustered index differs across database systems. Some systems organize table data directly around a clustered index, while others use different storage models.

sections.title: Non-Clustered Index
sections.content:
A non-clustered index provides a separate access structure from the primary table data.

Conceptually:

```text
Index
  |
  +----> Row/Page 10
  +----> Row/Page 35
  +----> Row/Page 82
```

The index can be searched efficiently, but the database may then need additional data-page accesses to retrieve columns that are not stored in the index.

If many matching rows are scattered across different pages, these additional lookups can become expensive.

sections.title: Composite Indexes
sections.content:
A composite index contains multiple columns.

For example:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_status
ON orders(customer_id, status);
```

This can help queries such as:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 101
  AND status = 'PAID';
```

Column order matters. An index on `(customer_id, status)` is organized differently from `(status, customer_id)`.

The best order depends on query patterns, selectivity, sorting requirements, and the database optimizer.

sections.title: Leftmost Prefix Rule
sections.content:
For a composite B-tree-style index such as:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_status_date
ON orders(customer_id, status, order_date);
```

The leading column has special importance. Queries filtering by `customer_id` can generally make use of the index effectively. Queries using `customer_id` and `status` can often use an even more specific prefix.

A query that only filters on `order_date` may not be able to use the index in the same efficient way.

This is commonly described as the leftmost-prefix principle, although exact optimizer behavior depends on the database engine.

sections.title: Covering Indexes
sections.content:
An index can be called covering for a query when the index contains all information needed to answer that query, allowing the database to avoid additional table-row lookups.

For example:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_name
ON users(email, name);
```

A query such as:

```sql
SELECT name
FROM users
WHERE email = 'user@example.com';
```

may be answerable entirely from the index, depending on the database engine and execution plan.

Covering indexes can reduce data-page access, but larger indexes consume more storage and increase write-maintenance cost.

sections.title: Index Selectivity
sections.content:
Selectivity describes how effectively a condition narrows down the number of matching rows.

A column with many distinct values often has higher selectivity than a column with only a few possible values.

For example:

```text
user_id -> millions of distinct values
status  -> 3 or 4 common values
```

An index on a highly selective column may be more useful for point lookups.

However, selectivity alone does not determine whether an index will be used. The optimizer also considers query predicates, statistics, data distribution, available indexes, estimated I/O, ordering, and the number of rows expected to be returned.

sections.title: Index Maintenance Cost
sections.content:
Indexes improve many read operations but are not free.

When a row is inserted, updated, or deleted, relevant indexes may also need to be modified.

```text
INSERT row
   |
   +----> Update table
   +----> Update index 1
   +----> Update index 2
   +----> Update index 3
```

Having too many indexes can increase write cost, storage consumption, cache pressure, and maintenance complexity.

Indexes should therefore be created based on real query patterns rather than adding an index to every column.

sections.title: What Is Query Processing?
sections.content:
Query processing is the process through which a DBMS converts a SQL statement into an executable strategy and produces the requested result.

A simplified pipeline is:

```text
SQL Query
   ↓
Parsing
   ↓
Validation
   ↓
Query Rewrite
   ↓
Optimization
   ↓
Execution Plan
   ↓
Execution
   ↓
Result
```

The database does not simply execute SQL text line by line. It builds an internal representation and chooses physical operations that it estimates will be efficient.

sections.title: SQL Parsing and Validation
sections.content:
The database first parses the SQL statement to determine its structure and verify that the syntax is valid.

It also validates objects, columns, data types, permissions, and other semantic requirements.

For example:

```sql
SELECT customer_id, total
FROM orders
WHERE total > 1000;
```

The database needs to identify the referenced table, columns, expressions, and filtering condition before it can generate an execution strategy.

sections.title: Query Rewrite
sections.content:
Before selecting a physical execution strategy, a DBMS may transform the query into an equivalent form that is easier or cheaper to execute.

Possible transformations include:

- Simplifying expressions.
- Removing unnecessary operations.
- Pushing filters closer to data access.
- Rewriting subqueries.
- Simplifying constant expressions.

For example, filtering rows earlier can reduce the amount of data that later operations such as joins or sorting need to process.

sections.title: Relational Query Operators
sections.content:
A query execution plan is composed of physical operations corresponding to relational operations.

Common operations include:

```text
Scan
Filter / Selection
Projection
Join
Sort
Aggregate
Group
Union
```

For example, a query such as:

```sql
SELECT customer_id
FROM orders
WHERE total > 1000;
```

can conceptually be represented as a scan followed by a filter and projection.

The database chooses physical implementations for these logical operations.

sections.title: Table Scan
sections.content:
A table scan reads table pages and examines rows to find those satisfying the query.

A full scan can be represented as:

```text
Table
  ↓
Page 1
Page 2
Page 3
...
Page N
  ↓
Filter rows
```

A table scan is not necessarily a bad execution strategy. It can be efficient when the query needs a large portion of the table or when the table is small enough that scanning it is cheaper than using an index.

sections.title: Index Scan and Index Seek
sections.content:
Database terminology differs between engines, but index-based access generally involves navigating an index to find relevant keys and then retrieving matching rows when necessary.

Conceptually:

```text
Query Predicate
      ↓
Index Navigation
      ↓
Matching Keys
      ↓
Data Pages
      ↓
Result
```

An index lookup can be very efficient for selective predicates. If a query matches a large percentage of the table, the optimizer may prefer a scan instead.

sections.title: Join Processing
sections.content:
Joins are among the most important and expensive operations in query processing.

Common physical join algorithms include:

```text
Nested Loop Join
Hash Join
Merge Join
```

The optimizer chooses among them based on factors such as table sizes, available indexes, ordering, join predicates, memory availability, and estimated result sizes.

For example, a hash join can be effective for equality joins when enough memory is available, while a merge join can be attractive when both inputs are already sorted appropriately.

sections.title: Nested Loop Join
sections.content:
A nested loop join conceptually processes one input and searches the other input for matching rows.

```text
For each row in outer table:
    Find matching rows in inner table
```

With an appropriate index on the inner table, nested loop joins can be very efficient when the outer input is small.

Without a useful index, repeatedly scanning the inner table can become expensive.

The optimizer therefore considers both estimated row counts and available access paths when choosing this algorithm.

sections.title: Hash Join
sections.content:
A hash join typically builds an in-memory hash structure for one input and probes it using rows from the other input.

Conceptually:

```text
Build Input
    ↓
Hash Table
    ↑
Probe Input
```

Hash joins are commonly useful for equality conditions such as:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c
  ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```

If the hash structure does not fit in memory, the database may need additional processing or temporary storage.

sections.title: Merge Join
sections.content:
A merge join processes two inputs that are ordered by their join keys and advances through them in order.

Conceptually:

```text
Input A: 10 20 30 40
Input B: 10 20 35 40
         ↓
Compare ordered keys
         ↓
Matching values
```

Merge joins can be efficient when inputs are already sorted or can be obtained efficiently in the required order.

Sorting the inputs first can add cost, so the optimizer evaluates whether a merge join is beneficial for the specific query.

sections.title: Sorting and Query Processing
sections.content:
Sorting is required or useful for operations such as `ORDER BY`, certain grouping operations, duplicate elimination, and some join strategies.

For example:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_date DESC;
```

If an appropriate index already provides rows in the required order, the database may avoid an explicit sort.

If sorting cannot be performed entirely in memory, the database may use temporary storage. This can significantly increase query cost for large datasets.

sections.title: Aggregation Processing
sections.content:
Aggregate queries use operations such as `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, and `MAX`.

For example:

```sql
SELECT customer_id, SUM(total)
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
```

The database may use hashing, sorting, indexes, or combinations of these techniques to compute the result.

The chosen strategy depends on the expected number of groups, available memory, data ordering, indexes, and optimizer estimates.

sections.title: Query Execution Plans
sections.content:
An execution plan describes the operations the database intends to perform for a query.

A simplified plan might look like:

```text
Aggregate
   |
Hash Join
  /    \
Scan   Index Scan
```

Execution plans can reveal whether the database is scanning a large table, using an index, performing an expensive sort, or choosing an unexpected join strategy.

Most database systems provide an `EXPLAIN` or similar command for inspecting plans.

sections.title: Using EXPLAIN
sections.content:
The `EXPLAIN` statement can be used to inspect how a database plans to execute a query.

For example, in systems that support this syntax:

```sql
EXPLAIN
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 101;
```

The output can contain information such as access method, estimated rows, chosen indexes, join strategy, and estimated cost.

Some database systems also provide commands such as `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` that execute the query and report actual runtime information. Because this executes the statement in many systems, it should be used carefully for queries that modify data or have expensive side effects.

sections.title: Cost-Based Query Optimization
sections.content:
Modern relational databases commonly use cost-based optimization. The optimizer estimates the cost of alternative execution plans and chooses a plan that it expects to be efficient.

A simplified process is:

```text
SQL Query
   ↓
Generate Candidate Plans
   ↓
Estimate Costs
   ↓
Compare Plans
   ↓
Choose Plan
```

Cost models can consider estimated I/O, CPU work, memory usage, row counts, join cardinality, available indexes, and other factors.

The chosen plan is based on estimates, so inaccurate statistics can cause the optimizer to make poor decisions.

sections.title: Database Statistics
sections.content:
Query optimizers rely on statistics to estimate data distribution and result sizes.

Statistics may describe information such as:

- Number of rows.
- Number of distinct values.
- Value distribution.
- Data density or selectivity estimates.
- Index characteristics.

For example, if the optimizer estimates that a predicate returns 10 rows but the actual query returns 500,000 rows, it may choose an inappropriate join or access strategy.

Keeping statistics reasonably current is therefore important for stable query performance.

sections.title: Cardinality Estimation
sections.content:
Cardinality estimation predicts how many rows an operation will produce.

For example:

```text
Orders table:       10,000,000 rows
Predicate estimate:       1,000 rows
Actual result:           900,000 rows
```

A large estimation error can cause the optimizer to choose an unsuitable execution plan.

Cardinality estimation is especially important for joins because an incorrect estimate early in the plan can affect many subsequent decisions.

sections.title: Predicate Pushdown
sections.content:
Predicate pushdown means applying filtering conditions as early as possible so later operations process fewer rows.

Suppose a query joins a large table and then filters it:

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'PAID';
```

If the database can filter `orders` by `status` before the join, the join may need to process fewer rows.

Reducing intermediate result sizes is one of the fundamental ideas behind efficient query execution.

sections.title: Projection Pushdown
sections.content:
Projection pushdown means retrieving only the columns needed by later operations or by the final result.

Instead of carrying every column through a complex execution plan, the database can sometimes discard unnecessary columns early.

For example:

```sql
SELECT customer_id
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'PAID';
```

There may be no reason for the execution engine to carry large unrelated columns through every intermediate step.

Reducing the amount of data processed can lower memory usage and I/O.

sections.title: Index Selection
sections.content:
When multiple indexes exist, the optimizer must determine whether an index is useful for the specific query.

For example:

```text
idx_customer_id
idx_status
idx_customer_status
idx_order_date
```

For a query filtering by both customer and status, a composite index may be more useful than an index on either column alone.

However, the optimizer also considers how many rows each option is expected to match, whether sorting can be avoided, whether the index covers required columns, and the cost of retrieving table rows.

sections.title: Sargable and Non-Sargable Predicates
sections.content:
A predicate is often called sargable when the database can efficiently use an index or other access method to search for matching values.

For example:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE email = 'user@example.com';
```

Applying a function directly to the indexed column can make efficient index access more difficult in some database systems:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE LOWER(email) = 'user@example.com';
```

The exact behavior depends on the database and available functional indexes or expression indexes. Query design should therefore be evaluated using the actual execution plan rather than assuming that every function prevents index usage.

sections.title: Pagination and Query Processing
sections.content:
Large result sets are commonly paginated.

Offset pagination is simple:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM orders
ORDER BY order_id
LIMIT 50 OFFSET 50000;
```

For large offsets, the database may still need to process or skip many earlier rows.

Keyset or cursor-based pagination can avoid large offsets:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE order_id > 50000
ORDER BY order_id
LIMIT 50;
```

With an appropriate index, keyset pagination can be much more efficient for deep pages and large datasets.

sections.title: Common Indexing Mistakes
sections.content:
Common indexing mistakes include:

- Creating indexes on every column without considering workload.
- Ignoring composite-index column order.
- Creating duplicate or overlapping indexes.
- Forgetting that indexes increase write cost.
- Assuming an index is always faster than a table scan.
- Ignoring data distribution and selectivity.
- Failing to inspect execution plans.
- Indexing columns that are rarely queried.
- Building very wide indexes without measuring their benefit.
- Forgetting to revisit indexes as application query patterns change.

sections.title: Common Query Processing Mistakes
sections.content:
Query-performance problems often come from inefficient access patterns rather than the database engine itself.

Common examples include:

- Selecting unnecessary columns.
- Returning millions of rows when only a small subset is required.
- Joining tables without appropriate predicates.
- Applying functions to columns unnecessarily.
- Using large offsets for deep pagination.
- Ignoring execution plans.
- Trusting outdated statistics.
- Assuming the same query plan is optimal for every data distribution.
- Performing repeated queries that could be combined or batched.

Performance tuning should be based on measurements and actual execution plans rather than assumptions.

sections.title: Practical Query Optimization Workflow
sections.content:
A practical optimization process can follow these steps:

```text
1. Identify the slow query
        ↓
2. Measure actual execution time
        ↓
3. Inspect EXPLAIN / execution plan
        ↓
4. Check estimated vs actual rows
        ↓
5. Inspect indexes and statistics
        ↓
6. Identify expensive operators
        ↓
7. Test a query or index change
        ↓
8. Measure again
        ↓
9. Validate write and storage impact
```

Do not optimize based only on intuition. A change that makes one query faster can increase write cost or make another important query slower.

The goal is to improve the workload as a whole, not just a single SQL statement.

sections.title: Storage, Indexing and Query Processing in Practice
sections.content:
Consider an order-management system with millions of records:

```sql
SELECT order_id, total, order_date
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 101
  AND status = 'PAID'
ORDER BY order_date DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

A suitable composite index might help the database locate orders for the customer and status while providing useful ordering information.

The database then evaluates the execution plan, estimates the number of matching rows, determines whether the index is beneficial, and retrieves only the required data.

A practical investigation should compare:

```text
No index
   ↓
Table scan

Composite index
   ↓
Index access
   ↓
Fewer pages / rows processed
```

The actual benefit must be measured using realistic data and workload characteristics.

sections.title: Why Storage, Indexing and Query Processing Matter
sections.content:
Storage, indexing, and query processing explain how a DBMS turns logical SQL statements into efficient physical operations.

The most important concepts are pages and blocks, buffer pools, file organization, indexes, B-tree and B+ tree structures, hash indexes, composite and covering indexes, selectivity, query execution plans, join algorithms, cost-based optimization, statistics, cardinality estimation, and predicate pushdown.

Good database performance is not achieved simply by adding indexes. It requires understanding how data is stored, how queries access that data, how the optimizer evaluates alternative plans, and how changes affect both reads and writes.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how databases store pages and records, use indexes, execute joins and scans, build query plans, and optimize SQL performance.
