topics.title: APPLIED DATABASE DESIGN AND ANALYSIS
topics.description: Learn how to turn real-world business requirements into reliable, scalable database designs. This topic covers requirement analysis, entity and relationship identification, schema design, normalization, keys and constraints, business rules, transaction boundaries, indexing, query patterns, denormalization, integrity, scalability, security, migration planning, and practical techniques for reviewing and improving database designs.

sections.title: What Is Applied Database Design?
sections.content:
Applied database design is the process of translating real-world requirements into a database structure that is correct, maintainable, and efficient. Instead of starting with tables immediately, a good design starts by understanding what the application needs to store and what operations it must perform.

A typical process is:

```text
Business Requirements
        ↓
Identify Data
        ↓
Identify Relationships
        ↓
Define Rules and Constraints
        ↓
Design Schema
        ↓
Normalize
        ↓
Design Indexes
        ↓
Test Queries and Workload
        ↓
Review and Improve
```

Applied design connects database theory with practical application development.

sections.title: Start With Requirements
sections.content:
A database design should begin with requirements rather than SQL statements. For an e-commerce application, requirements might include:

- Customers can create accounts.
- Customers can place orders.
- An order contains multiple products.
- Products have prices and inventory.
- Payments have a status.
- Orders can be cancelled according to business rules.

These statements describe business behavior. The database designer must translate them into entities, attributes, relationships, and constraints.

A poorly understood requirement can lead to a technically valid schema that does not correctly represent the application.

sections.title: Identify Entities
sections.content:
An entity represents a distinct object or concept that the application needs to store information about.

For an online store, possible entities include:

```text
Customer
Product
Order
OrderItem
Payment
Address
```

A useful question is: Does this concept have its own identity and lifecycle in the application?

For example, a customer can exist independently of an individual order, so Customer is usually a separate entity.

sections.title: Identify Attributes
sections.content:
After identifying entities, determine the properties that need to be stored for each entity.

For example:

```text
Customer
- customer_id
- name
- email
- created_at

Product
- product_id
- name
- price
- stock_quantity
```

Attributes should represent information that the application actually needs. Avoid storing the same fact repeatedly in unrelated tables unless there is a deliberate reason, because duplicated data can become inconsistent.

sections.title: Identify Relationships
sections.content:
Relationships describe how entities are connected.

For example:

```text
Customer 1 ---- N Order
Order    1 ---- N OrderItem
Product  1 ---- N OrderItem
```

This means one customer can have many orders, one order can contain many order items, and one product can appear in many order items.

Relationships should be derived from actual business rules rather than assumptions about how tables might be convenient to implement.

sections.title: Cardinality and Participation
sections.content:
Cardinality describes how many instances of one entity can be associated with another entity.

Common relationships include:

```text
1 : 1  -> One-to-One
1 : N  -> One-to-Many
N : M  -> Many-to-Many
```

You should also determine whether participation is mandatory or optional.

For example, if every order must belong to a customer, an order's customer relationship is mandatory. If a customer may exist without placing an order, the customer-to-order relationship is optional from the customer's perspective.

sections.title: Mapping Relationships to Tables
sections.content:
Relationships in the conceptual model must eventually become relational structures. A one-to-many relationship is usually represented using a foreign key on the many side.

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    order_date TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
);
```

Here, many orders can reference the same customer. A many-to-many relationship normally requires an associative or junction table.

sections.title: Designing Primary Keys
sections.content:
Every important entity should have a reliable way to identify its records. A primary key should generally be unique, stable, non-null, and suitable for the workload.

For example:

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);
```

The choice between generated numeric identifiers, UUIDs, natural keys, and composite keys depends on system requirements such as distribution, integration, storage size, and operational constraints.

sections.title: Natural Keys vs Surrogate Keys
sections.content:
A natural key is based on a meaningful business value, while a surrogate key is an artificial identifier generated specifically for database identity.

For example:

```text
Natural key:
email

Surrogate key:
customer_id
```

Natural values can change or may have business-specific complications. Surrogate keys can provide stable internal references while a separate unique constraint protects the business identifier.

There is no universal rule that one approach is always correct. The choice should be based on identity semantics, integration requirements, and expected changes.

sections.title: Foreign Keys and Referential Integrity
sections.content:
Foreign keys enforce relationships between tables and help prevent invalid references.

For example:

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
        REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
);
```

This prevents an order from referencing a customer that does not exist, subject to the database's constraint behavior.

Foreign keys are an important database-level defense against inconsistent relationships, even when the application also performs validation.

sections.title: Choosing Data Types
sections.content:
Choosing appropriate data types affects correctness, storage, indexing, and query behavior.

For example:

```text
Quantity       -> integer type
Price          -> exact numeric type
Created time   -> timestamp/date-time type
Status         -> constrained string or database-specific enum/domain
Identifier     -> integer, UUID, or another appropriate identifier type
```

Money should generally use an exact numeric representation rather than floating-point arithmetic when precise financial values are required.

Do not select extremely large data types without a reason, but also avoid types that cannot represent the required range or precision.

sections.title: Constraints as Business Rules
sections.content:
Constraints allow important rules to be enforced close to the data.

Common constraints include:

```text
PRIMARY KEY
FOREIGN KEY
UNIQUE
NOT NULL
CHECK
```

For example:

```sql
CREATE TABLE products (
    product_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    price DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
    stock_quantity INT NOT NULL CHECK (stock_quantity >= 0)
);
```

Database constraints provide a final integrity boundary even when multiple applications or services write to the same database.

sections.title: Normalization in Applied Design
sections.content:
Normalization helps organize data so that each fact is stored in an appropriate place and unnecessary dependencies are reduced.

For example, instead of storing customer information repeatedly in every order:

```text
Orders
order_id | customer_id | customer_name
```

use separate entities:

```text
Customers
customer_id | customer_name

Orders
order_id | customer_id
```

Normalization reduces update anomalies and improves data consistency.

The appropriate level of normalization depends on workload and application requirements. Practical systems sometimes deliberately denormalize selected data for performance or reporting.

sections.title: Functional Dependencies in Design
sections.content:
Functional dependencies help determine whether attributes belong together in the same relation.

If a customer ID uniquely determines a customer email:

```text
customer_id -> email
```

then storing unrelated customer attributes repeatedly in an order table may introduce redundancy.

Functional dependency analysis is particularly useful when deciding whether a schema satisfies higher normal forms and when identifying attributes that depend on only part of a composite key.

sections.title: Avoiding Redundant Data
sections.content:
Redundant data occurs when the same fact is unnecessarily stored in multiple places.

For example:

```text
Order 101 -> Customer Name = Amit
Order 102 -> Customer Name = Amit
Order 103 -> Customer Name = Amit
```

If the customer's name changes, multiple records may need to be updated.

A normalized design stores the customer once and references the customer from orders.

Some duplication can be intentional, such as storing a historical snapshot of an address on an invoice. The important distinction is whether the duplication represents a deliberate business requirement or accidental redundancy.

sections.title: Handling Historical Data
sections.content:
Current entity state and historical business records often have different requirements.

For example, an invoice may need to preserve the customer's billing address at the time the invoice was created, even if the customer later changes their address.

Therefore, copying an address into an invoice is not necessarily bad normalization. It can represent historical truth.

A practical design should distinguish between:

```text
Current state
vs
Historical snapshot
```

Database design must represent the business meaning of the data, not blindly eliminate every duplicated value.

sections.title: Designing Status and Lifecycle Fields
sections.content:
Many business entities have lifecycle states.

For example:

```text
PENDING
    ↓
CONFIRMED
    ↓
PROCESSING
    ↓
COMPLETED
```

A status column can represent the current state, but the design should also consider whether the application needs a complete history of state changes.

If auditing is required, a separate history table may be appropriate:

```text
order_status_history
- id
- order_id
- old_status
- new_status
- changed_at
- changed_by
```

This allows the current state and historical events to serve different purposes.

sections.title: Temporal and Audit Requirements
sections.content:
Many production systems need to answer questions such as: When was this record created? Who changed it? What was its previous value? When did a status change occur?

Common audit fields include:

```text
created_at
created_by
updated_at
updated_by
```

More detailed audit requirements may require separate audit tables or event records.

Audit design should be considered early because reconstructing historical information after the fact can be difficult if the original changes were not captured.

sections.title: Designing for Transactions
sections.content:
Database structure should support the application's transaction boundaries.

Suppose placing an order requires:

```text
Create Order
Reserve Inventory
Create Order Items
Create Payment Record
```

If these operations must succeed together, the schema should allow them to participate in one coherent transaction.

Poor schema boundaries can force an application to perform partial updates across unrelated structures, increasing the risk of inconsistent state.

Database design and transaction design should therefore be considered together.

sections.title: Concurrency-Aware Database Design
sections.content:
A schema should also consider what happens when multiple requests modify the same data simultaneously.

For example, two users may attempt to purchase the last available item.

A simple read-then-write sequence can create a race condition:

```text
T1: Read stock = 1
T2: Read stock = 1
T1: Reduce stock to 0
T2: Reduce stock to 0
```

The design may require transactions, row-level locking, atomic updates, optimistic version checks, or other concurrency-control mechanisms.

Database design should therefore account for concurrent workloads rather than only the single-user case.

sections.title: Designing Indexes From Query Patterns
sections.content:
Indexes should be derived from actual application access patterns.

Start with important queries:

```sql
SELECT order_id, total
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 101
ORDER BY order_date DESC;
```

A possible index might be:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_date
ON orders(customer_id, order_date);
```

The exact index should be validated using execution plans and realistic data.

Do not design indexes only from the table structure. The same table may require very different indexes depending on how the application searches, joins, sorts, and filters its data.

sections.title: Composite Index Design
sections.content:
Composite indexes contain multiple columns and are especially useful when queries repeatedly filter or sort by combinations of fields.

For example:

```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_status_date
ON orders(customer_id, status, order_date);
```

The order of columns matters because the index has an ordered structure.

Consider:

```text
(customer_id, status, order_date)
```

This is not equivalent to:

```text
(status, customer_id, order_date)
```

Index column order should be chosen based on query predicates, ordering requirements, selectivity, and workload measurements.

sections.title: Query-Driven Schema Design
sections.content:
Database design should balance normalized data structures with the queries the application must execute.

For example, a reporting system may frequently ask:

```sql
SELECT customer_id, SUM(total)
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_id;
```

The design should consider how this query will access the data, whether appropriate indexes exist, and whether aggregation over the operational schema is acceptable.

The goal is not to design tables independently from queries. A production database is a combination of data model and access patterns.

sections.title: When to Denormalize
sections.content:
Denormalization intentionally duplicates or precomputes information to improve performance or simplify specific workloads.

For example, an order table might store a calculated total:

```text
Order
- order_id
- customer_id
- total_amount
```

instead of calculating it from every order item for every read.

Denormalization introduces a consistency responsibility. If the underlying items change, the stored total must also remain correct.

A good approach is to normalize first, measure actual performance problems, and then introduce targeted denormalization where the benefit justifies the additional complexity.

sections.title: Read Models and Reporting Tables
sections.content:
Operational databases are optimized for transactional workloads, while reporting workloads may require large scans, aggregations, and historical analysis.

Instead of forcing complex analytics onto the transactional schema, systems may create dedicated reporting structures.

Conceptually:

```text
Transactional Database
        |
        v
Reporting / Analytical Model
        |
        v
Dashboards and Reports
```

This separation can protect transactional workloads from expensive analytical queries.

The appropriate architecture depends on data volume, freshness requirements, complexity, and operational constraints.

sections.title: Database Design for High-Write Systems
sections.content:
Write-heavy applications require special attention to index count, transaction duration, contention, and storage growth.

For example, a high-volume event table may receive thousands of inserts per second.

Every additional index can increase write maintenance work.

A practical design should consider:

```text
Insert throughput
Index maintenance
Transaction size
Lock contention
Storage growth
Partitioning requirements
Retention policy
```

The goal is to keep the write path efficient while preserving the indexes and constraints required for correctness and important reads.

sections.title: Partitioning Considerations
sections.content:
Partitioning divides a large logical table into smaller physical partitions according to a partitioning strategy.

A common example is partitioning time-based data by month:

```text
orders_2026_01
orders_2026_02
orders_2026_03
...
```

The actual implementation is usually managed by the database rather than separate application tables.

Partitioning can help with very large datasets, data lifecycle management, and queries that naturally restrict data to specific partitions.

It is not a replacement for indexing and should be introduced only when workload characteristics justify it.

sections.title: Data Retention and Archiving
sections.content:
Production databases often contain data that becomes less frequently accessed over time.

For example:

```text
Hot Data      -> Frequently accessed
Warm Data     -> Occasionally accessed
Cold Data     -> Rarely accessed / archived
```

A retention strategy defines how long data remains in the primary database and when older records are archived or deleted.

Retention policies can reduce storage growth and improve operational performance, but they must respect legal, business, audit, and recovery requirements.

sections.title: Database Security by Design
sections.content:
Security should be part of database design rather than added after implementation.

Important considerations include:

- Least-privilege database users.
- Strong authentication.
- Encryption where required.
- Sensitive-data protection.
- Secure connection configuration.
- Auditing.
- Safe parameterized queries.
- Appropriate access boundaries.

For example, an application account should generally receive only the database permissions required for its workload rather than unrestricted administrative privileges.

sections.title: Handling Sensitive Data
sections.content:
Sensitive information should be identified during requirements analysis.

Examples can include:

```text
Personal information
Authentication data
Payment-related information
Business secrets
Private customer records
```

The design may require encryption, tokenization, masking, restricted access, audit logging, or separate storage depending on the sensitivity and applicable requirements.

Passwords should never be stored as reversible plaintext values. Authentication systems should use appropriate password hashing mechanisms rather than ordinary database encryption.

sections.title: Schema Evolution
sections.content:
Production database schemas change over time as applications evolve.

Examples include:

```text
Add column
Add index
Create table
Rename field
Change data type
Split table
Merge structures
```

Schema changes should be planned so that application deployments do not unexpectedly break existing code.

For larger systems, backward-compatible migrations are often useful:

```text
Deploy schema change
        ↓
Deploy application supporting old + new schema
        ↓
Migrate data
        ↓
Switch reads/writes
        ↓
Remove old structure later
```

The exact migration strategy depends on application architecture and database capabilities.

sections.title: Migration Safety
sections.content:
Database migrations can be risky when they operate on large production tables.

A seemingly simple operation can require substantial work:

```sql
ALTER TABLE orders
ADD COLUMN processing_status VARCHAR(30);
```

The impact depends on the database engine, table size, existing indexes, locking behavior, and the specific schema operation.

Safe migration planning should consider execution time, locking, rollback strategy, compatibility with application versions, backups, and monitoring.

Large migrations should be tested against production-like data before deployment.

sections.title: Database Design Review
sections.content:
A database design review should examine more than whether the tables are syntactically valid.

A practical review can ask:

```text
Are entities correctly identified?
Are relationships correct?
Are keys stable?
Are constraints sufficient?
Is unnecessary duplication present?
Are transaction boundaries supported?
Are important queries indexed?
Will writes remain efficient?
How will data grow?
How will old data be archived?
How will failures be recovered?
How will schema changes be deployed?
```

Reviewing the design from both a data-integrity and workload perspective catches problems before they become expensive production issues.

sections.title: Analyzing a Practical Order Database
sections.content:
Consider an order-processing system with these entities:

```text
Customer
Product
Order
OrderItem
Payment
```

A reasonable relationship model is:

```text
Customer 1 ---- N Order
Order    1 ---- N OrderItem
Product  1 ---- N OrderItem
Order    1 ---- N Payment
```

A simplified schema could be:

```sql
CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_item_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    product_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    quantity INT NOT NULL,
    unit_price DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
    FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(order_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products(product_id)
);
```

Notice that unit_price can intentionally preserve the price used for the order rather than always reading the product's current price. This is a practical example of storing historical business information.

sections.title: Analyzing Database Workload
sections.content:
A schema should be evaluated against the workload it will actually receive.

Classify important operations as:

```text
Read-heavy
Write-heavy
Mixed
Transactional
Analytical
Batch
Real-time
```

Then examine:

- Most frequent queries.
- Slowest queries.
- Largest tables.
- Highest-write tables.
- Most frequently updated rows.
- Important transaction paths.
- Data growth rate.

This analysis helps determine where indexes, caching, partitioning, denormalization, replicas, or separate analytical structures may be appropriate.

sections.title: Performance Testing a Database Design
sections.content:
Database performance should be tested using realistic data volume and realistic query patterns.

A design that performs well with 10,000 rows may behave very differently with 100 million rows.

A useful test process is:

```text
Representative Data
        ↓
Representative Queries
        ↓
Concurrent Load
        ↓
Measure Latency
        ↓
Inspect Execution Plans
        ↓
Measure CPU / I/O / Memory
        ↓
Tune
        ↓
Retest
```

Performance testing should include both normal workload and important peak scenarios.

sections.title: Common Database Design Mistakes
sections.content:
Common design mistakes include:

- Designing tables before understanding requirements.
- Storing multiple values in a single column.
- Missing foreign-key relationships.
- Using inappropriate data types.
- Storing duplicated business data without a reason.
- Adding indexes without analyzing queries.
- Creating too many indexes on write-heavy tables.
- Ignoring historical data requirements.
- Treating current state and event history as the same thing.
- Ignoring concurrent updates.
- Using database constraints inconsistently.
- Making large schema changes without migration planning.
- Optimizing for today's data volume without considering growth.
- Assuming normalization or denormalization is always the correct answer.

sections.title: Applied Database Design Workflow
sections.content:
A repeatable database design workflow can be summarized as:

```text
1. Gather requirements
        ↓
2. Identify entities and business concepts
        ↓
3. Identify relationships
        ↓
4. Define keys and constraints
        ↓
5. Normalize the model
        ↓
6. Define transaction boundaries
        ↓
7. Identify important queries
        ↓
8. Design indexes
        ↓
9. Consider growth and retention
        ↓
10. Consider security and recovery
        ↓
11. Test with realistic workload
        ↓
12. Review and iterate
```

Database design is iterative. Requirements, workload, data volume, and application architecture can all change, so a good schema should be reviewed as the system evolves.

sections.title: From Requirements to Production Schema
sections.content:
A production-ready database design connects several layers of reasoning.

```text
Business Requirement
        ↓
Conceptual Model
        ↓
ER Design
        ↓
Relational Schema
        ↓
Normalization
        ↓
Constraints
        ↓
Indexes
        ↓
Transactions
        ↓
Queries
        ↓
Performance Testing
        ↓
Production
```

A schema should not be considered complete merely because its tables can be created successfully. It should also represent the business correctly, protect data integrity, support important queries, handle concurrency, and remain manageable as the system grows.

sections.title: Why Applied Database Design and Analysis Matter
sections.content:
Applied database design brings together the major concepts of database engineering: requirements analysis, entity modeling, normalization, keys, constraints, transactions, concurrency, indexing, query patterns, security, scalability, and operational maintenance.

The goal is not simply to create tables. The goal is to create a data model that remains correct and useful under real application workloads.

A strong design answers three questions:

```text
Is the data modeled correctly?
        ↓
Is the data protected from invalid states?
        ↓
Can the system access and maintain the data efficiently?
```

These questions provide a practical framework for evaluating database designs before and after they reach production.
